The longest worm that can infect humans is Taenia saginata, also known as the beef tapeworm. It is known for its substantial length, capable of reaching up to 25 meters.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old pregnant woman presents to your clinic with a two-week history of swollen lymph nodes in her neck. She reports no fever, night sweats, or weight loss. Her obstetric history reveals that she is currently in her second trimester. She mentions owning a cat and often handling the cat litter. An ultrasound of the fetus shows intracranial calcifications. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

quot;Calibri",sans-serif">MC manifestation: Chorioretinitis

  • More chance of infection: 3rd trimester.

    Option A. Cytomegalovirus infection: This can cause congenital infections, but the specific association with cat litter and intracranial calcifications is more indicative of toxoplasmosis.

     

    Option C. Rubella: While rubella can cause congenital defects, it is typically associated with cataracts, heart defects, and hearing impairment, not specifically intracranial calcifications.

questions.stem: A newborn is suspected of having congenital toxoplasmosis. Which of the following laboratory findings would most reliably confirm the diagnosis in the neonate?

options.label: A
options.text: IgM antibodies against Toxoplasma in the mother

options.label: B
options.text: IgM antibodies against Toxoplasma in the fetus

options.label: C
options.text: IgG antibodies against Toxoplasma in the mother

options.label: D
options.text: IgG antibodies against Toxoplasma in the fetus

questions.answerText: IgM antibodies against Toxoplasma in the fetus
questions.solutionHtml:
suggests an in utero infection.

 

Explanation:

 

Option A) IgM in the mother: Maternal IgM indicates exposure but does not confirm fetal infection.

 

Option C) IgG in the mother: IgG antibodies can cross the placenta, so their presence in the mother is not specific for congenital infection.

 

Option D) IgG in the fetus: IgG antibodies can be transferred from the mother to the fetus and do not necessarily indicate fetal infection.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The detection of IgM antibodies against Toxoplasma in a newborn indicates congenital infection, as IgM doesn't cross the placenta, meaning these antibodies must have been produced by the fetus itself. Other indicators, like maternal IgM or IgG, don't confirm fetal infection since IgG can cross the placenta and maternal IgM only shows the mother's exposure. Fetal IgG also doesn't necessarily indicate infection, as these could be antibodies passed from the mother.

 

Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Parasitology 2/e p99



Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Parasitology 2/e p99

questions.stem: A public health officer is investigating a cluster of toxoplasmosis cases in a suburban area. Which of the following is the most likely reservoir for Toxoplasma gondii in this scenario?
questions.solutionHtml:
le="font-family:"Calibri",sans-serif">Explanation:

 

Option B) Bats: Bats are not known to be a reservoir for Toxoplasma gondii.

 

Option C) Raccoons: While raccoons can carry various parasites, they are not the primary reservoir for toxoplasmosis.

 

Option D) Pigeons: Pigeons are not reservoirs for Toxoplasma gondii.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The life cycle of Toxoplasma gondii involves two hosts:

 

  •  Definitive hosts are cat and other felines; where the sexual cycle takes place.
  • Intermediate hosts are man and other mammals (goat, sheep, pig, cattle and certain birds); where the asexual cycle takes place.

 

Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Parasitology 1/e p120, 2/e p94

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman with a history of rheumatoid arthritis treated with methotrexate and prednisone presents with confusion, fever, and headache. Brain MRI shows multiple ring-enhancing lesions. Serology tests for Toxoplasma gondii come back positive. Which of the following statements about Toxoplasma gondii in this context is true?

options.label: A
options.text: Direct spread by blood/urine is the main mode of transmission

options.label: B
options.text: Cerebellum is the most common site of brain involvement

options.label: C
options.text: Isolation of the parasite from blood is very easy

options.label: D
options.text: Laboratory tests are useful for making a diagnosis

questions.answerText: Laboratory tests are useful for making a diagnosis
questions.solutionHtml:
tyle="font-family:"Calibri",sans-serif">Serological procedures have great diagnostic value and has become the routine method of diagnosis.

 

Explanation:

 

Option A) Direct spread by blood/urine:  The principal route of human toxoplasma infection is by the oral route by ingestion of either sporulated oocysts from contaminated soil, food, or water or bradyzoites from undercooked meat. Other Route-Transmission Via Blood or Organs and Transplacental Transmission

 

Option B) Cerebellum: Although lesions can occur anywhere in the CNS, the areas most often involved appear to be the brainstem, basal ganglia, pituitary gland, and corticomedullary junction.

 

Option C) Isolation of the parasite: Although difficult and available only at specialized laboratories, the isolation of T. gondii from blood or other body fluids can be accomplished

 

Educational Objective:

 

In immunocompromised individuals, such as those on immunosuppressive therapy, Toxoplasma gondii infection can be severe and progressive, leading to neurological symptoms consistent with cerebral toxoplasmosis. Laboratory tests are crucial for diagnosis, and serological procedures are commonly used for this purpose. While direct spread by blood/urine, the involvement of the cerebellum, and parasite isolation not relevant for the diagnosis and severity assessment of cerebral toxoplasmosis in immunocompromised individuals.

 

Ref: Harrison 18/e p1723-28; Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Parasitology 1/e p121-124, 2/e p94-99

questions.stemHtml: A 42-year-old male with a history of advanced HIV/AIDS presents to the emergency department with a two-week history of altered mental status, including confusion, disorientation, and generalized weakness. His partner reports that he has been increasingly lethargic and less responsive. Physical examination reveals no focal neurological deficits. Laboratory investigations show a CD4 count of 30 cells/mm³. A blood smear examination is performed, revealing the following: Which of the following parasites is most likely responsible for his condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
pan style="font-size:11pt">Figure: B.Histopathology of brain shows pseudocyst containing numerous tachyzoites; C. Tissue cyst containing bradyzoites (section of brain stained with hematoxylin and eosin)

 

Explanation:

 

Option B) Sarcocystis: This parasite does not typically cause encephalopathy.

 

Option C) Plasmodium: Causes malaria, which has a different clinical presentation and smear findings.

 

Option D) Trypanosoma: Causes trypanosomiasis, which presents differently and has distinct smear findings.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In immunosuppressed individuals, especially those with advanced HIV/AIDS and low CD4 counts, Toxoplasma gondii can cause cerebral toxoplasmosis, leading to encephalopathy. The presence of tachyzoites in the peripheral blood is indicative of active toxoplasmosis. Sarcocystis spp., Plasmodium spp. (causing malariA), and Trypanosoma spp. (causing trypanosomiasis) have different clinical presentations and are not typically associated with tachyzoites in the blood. 

 

Ref: Paniker’s parasitology 7/e p91, Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Parasitology, 1e/p123-4,2e/p97-98

questions.stem: A 25-year-old male presents with abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea. He recently returned from a trip to a tropical country. On examination, his stool sample reveals trophozoites with ingested red blood cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
span style="font-size:12.0pt">Explanation:

 

Option A) Giardia lamblia: Incorrect, as it usually causes non-bloody diarrhea and does not ingest red blood cells.

Option D) Clostridium perfringens: Incorrect, as it typically causes food poisoning with watery diarrhea but not dysentery with ingested red blood cells.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Entamoeba histolytica - This organism is specifically known for causing dysentery and trophozoites with ingestion of red blood cells is a classic indication of its infection.

questions.stemHtml: A 23-year-old male with a one-week history of abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea undergoes a colonoscopic biopsy. The biopsy results suggest an infection. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis based on these findings?
questions.solutionHtml:
le="font-size:11pt">Explanation:

 

Option A) Giardiasis: Incorrect, as Giardia lamblia typically causes non-bloody diarrhea and is not usually diagnosed via colonoscopic biopsy.

 

Option C) Enterobius (pinworm): Incorrect, as Enterobius vermicularis mainly causes perianal pruritus and is unlikely to cause bloody diarrhea or be diagnosed through a colonoscopic biopsy.

 

Option D) Severe bacterial infection: Incorrect, as bacterial infections usually present with a different set of histopathological findings on biopsy.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The clinical presentation and diagnostic findings consistent with amoebiasis, including abdominal pain, bloody diarrhea, and colonoscopic biopsy results indicating an infectious process.

questions.stem: A researcher is studying the pathogenesis of Entamoeba histolytica. Which virulence factor is primarily responsible for the adherence of this parasite to the intestinal mucosa?
questions.solutionHtml:
oebiasis, leading to tissue invasion and symptom development.

 

Explanation:

 

Option A) Ionophore-like protein: Incorrect, as this is not primarily involved in adherence to the intestinal mucosa.

 

Option C) Phosphatase: Incorrect, while enzymes like phosphatase may play a role in the lifecycle, they are not mainly responsible for mucosal adherence.

 

Option D) Proteinase: Incorrect, although proteinases may contribute to tissue invasion and damage, they are not the primary factor for adherence.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Amoebic lectin antigen is the principal virulence factor of Entamoeba histolytica that is responsible for adherence to large intestinal mucosa. Ionophore-like protein, Phosphatase, and Proteinase, while they may have roles in the amoeba's lifecycle and pathogenesis, are not primarily responsible for mucosal adherence.

 

Ref: Apurba Sastry’s Essentials of Medical Parasitology 1/e p29, 2/e p20

questions.stem: Which statement is true regarding Acute Primary Amoebic Meningoencephalitis (PAM)?

options.label: A
options.text: Meningitis caused by Acanthamoeba species is acute in nature

options.label: B
options.text: Diagnosis is by demonstration of trophozoite in CSF

questions.answerText: Diagnosis is by demonstration of trophozoite in CSF
questions.solutionHtml:
lic/images/2024/03/05/screenshot-2024-03-05-100242.jpg" alt="" width="1000" height="495">

 

Explanation:

 

Option A) Meningitis caused by Acanthamoeba species is acute in nature: Incorrect, as Acanthamoeba infections are typically not acute and can be chronic or subacute  and it causes Granulomatous meningoencephalitis not primary meningoencephalitis as mentioned in the question.

 

Option C) Caused by feco-oral transmission: Incorrect, as PAM is not transmitted through the feco-oral route rather naegleria fowleri enters via the nasal route,. It’s commonly associated with swimming in warm freshwater.

Educational Objective:

 

Primary Amoebic meningoencephalitis

 

  • Caused by Naegleria fowleri, which is acute and suppurative in nature (Granulomatous amoebic encephalitis caused by Acanthamoeba species is chronic in nature)

  • Diagnosis is by demonstration of trophozoite in CSF (GAE is diagnosed by demonstration of both Acanthamoeba trophozoite and cyst in CSF)

  • Transmitted by: Nasal route (Acanthamoeba by Respiratory or rarely through skin penetration)

questions.stem: A 35-year-old male in India presents to the emergency department with a 2-day history of high fever, severe headache, and episodes of vomiting. He has recently returned from a rural area with known malaria transmission. On examination, he is febrile (39.5°C, disoriented, and experiencing seizures. Laboratory tests confirm a high parasitemia of Plasmodium falciparum. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
span>

 

Option A. Viral encephalitis – Although presenting with similar neurological symptoms, the presence of high P. falciparum parasitemia makes cerebral malaria more likely.

 

Option B. Bacterial meningitis – Meningitis typically presents with neck stiffness, photophobia, and might not coincide with P. falciparum parasitemia.

 

Option D. Heat stroke – While it can cause altered mental status and high body temperature, it does not explain the high parasitemia.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Cerebral malaria, linked to P. falciparum infection, is marked by seizures, altered consciousness, and high fever. It involves the sequestration of parasitized RBCs in brain capillaries, causing vascular occlusion and cerebral anoxia. This condition, more common in children, can lead to encephalopathy, retinal hemorrhages, and a high mortality rate. Diagnosis is typically made through peripheral blood smear examination, revealing characteristic P. falciparum forms.

Lung flukes can lead to cavitary lesions, but they don't form two-layered cystic structures. Strongyloides doesn't create cystic structures in the lungs.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man presents with fatigue and pallor. He is an avid consumer of sushi and other raw fish dishes. Laboratory tests reveal macrocytic anemia. A stool examination shows distinctive eggs. Considering his dietary habits and the lab findings, which statement is true about the parasite suspected in his condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
trong>Figure: A. Scolex, carmine-stained; B. Egg of Diphyllobothrium latum—note the operculum (red arrow) and posterior knob (black arrow); C. Carmine-stained gravid proglottids of Diphyllobothrium latum (broader than longer, rosette-shaped ovaries)

 

Explanation:

 

Option A. Man is a single host: Incorrect, as man is the definitive host, but there are intermediate hosts in the lifecycle.

 

Option B. Iron deficiency anemia: Diphyllobothrium latum primarily causes vitamin B₁₂ deficiency anemia (megaloblastic or macrocytic anemia) rather than iron deficiency anemia. 

 

Option D. Fish is the definitive host: Fish are intermediate hosts; humans are the definitive hosts.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Diphyllobothrium latum (fish tapeworm) causes vitamin B12 deficiency anemia, not iron deficiency anemia. This is due to the tapeworm's ability to absorb vitamin B12 in the intestine. Humans are the definitive hosts with multiple intermediate hosts involved in its lifecycle, not making man a single host. The eggs of Diphyllobothrium are non-operculated and fish serve as intermediate hosts in the life cycle of Diphyllobothrium, while humans are the definitive hosts. Operculated eggs in the stool is diagnostic of an infection with Diphyllobothrium latum.
